newsitem.title: FRANCE: Italy, France, Germany close in EMU race - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Italy, France, Germany close in EMU race - OECD.

text.p: Italy, France and Germany are likely to be neck-in-neck in the race to cut their budget deficits and qualify for monetary union, according to forecasts published by the OECD on Thursday.
The Paris-based Western economic thinktank forecast all three would show a total public deficit of 3.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1997.
This is just shy of a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty which calls for deficits to be reduced to three percent of GDP by this year.
But the OECD's chief economist said the decision, due to be taken in April/May 1998, on which countries qualify for economic and monetary union in 1999 should not be based on decimal points.
"The decision will be political," Stephen Potter told a news conference. "From an economic point of view, it would seem anomalous to exclude a few countries on the basis of a few decimal points."

Potter said it was above all the downward trend in deficits which counted. Although the OECD forecast showed Italy's deficit rising in 1998, Potter added: "By the time the decisions are made Italy will have had time to take further action."
Asked to assess the risks if monetary union did not happen, Potter said:

"We would see the risk of quite strong financial market disturbances. The markets have been expecting EMU and long term interest rates have come down, decreasing differentials with Germany and exchange rates have been stable."

"One could see the risk of a reversal on both those counts, an increase in long-term interest rates outside Germany. And Germany would be bound to suffer from the more unstable environment, (although) the mark might tend to strengthen."
The OECD (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development) forecasts, which some economists said may already be outdated, had little impact on financial markets.
But economists said they pointed to broad EMU membership, rather than the narrow one sought by Bonn, trying to cut its deficit to 3.0 percent to ensure a strict reading of Maastricht.
"It's not bad enough to provoke thoughts of delay (in EMU)," Nomura economist Sonja Gibbs said. "On the face of it, if it has any impact at all, it is definitely broad EMU-friendly."

The OECD also forecast, in its half-year economic outlook, that Germany and France would cut their deficits further in 1998, to 2.7 and 3.0 percent of GDP respectively. But Italy's deficit/GDP ratio was seen rising to 3.8 percent.
Officials have recently been insisting that deficit cuts must be sustainable, in what some see as a warning to Italy it may be left out of EMU if it cannot keep up its 1997 performance.

The OECD's 1998 forecast for Italy, however, did not take account of a three-year plan Rome has promised to cut its debt and deficit, nor of a likely fall in Italian interest rates if it does make it into EMU in 1999.
"I think (the forecasts) are quite bullish for Italy," UBS economist Darren Williams said.
Spain and Portugal, meanwhile, whose chances of joining EMU in 1999 are often seen as linked to Italy's success in getting in, were given top EMU marks by the OECD.
It saw Spain's deficit/GDP ratio at 3.0 percent in 1997 and 2.6 percent in 1998, and Portugal's at 2.9 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998.
Spain's determination to join EMU in 1999 has been a key factor in convincing Italy it must not be left behind.

Economists said in any case the deficit/GDP ratios probably mattered less than political developments in Europe, particularly in France where the new Socialist-led government has been fighting to water down EU austerity policies.

France has said it wants Italy and Spain to join EMU at the start, that there should be a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty, and that it will not impose new austerity just to cut the deficit/GDP ratio to exactly 3.0 percent.
"The ball is still in France's court," Gibbs said.
